sources.cite: NIMH, Ask Suicide-Screening Questions (ASQ) Toolkit, information sheet: four questions and a fifth acuity question asked after any yes; a yes to it is an acute positive, 'imminent risk', that needs a STAT safety and full mental health evaluation, and the patient 'cannot leave until evaluated for safety'; a non-acute positive needs a brief suicide safety assessment; refusing to answer counts as positive
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 in NIMH's PDF (summarizing fetch with short quotes). The four questions: a wish to be dead, feeling others would be better off, thoughts of suicide in the past week, any attempt ever. 'Clinical judgment can always override a negative screen.' Validated for youth and adult medical patients, including adult medical inpatients (Horowitz et al., Psychosomatics 2020); the toolkit has emergency department, inpatient and outpatient pathways (NIMH adult toolkit page, read the same day). The questions are paraphrased in the sim.

sources.cite: NIMH, Adult ASQ Toolkit: Brief Suicide Safety Assessment guides, nursing scripts and suicide risk screening pathways for the emergency department, the inpatient medical/surgical unit and outpatient primary care and specialty clinics
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 (summarizing fetch): an index page; the pathways themselves were not opened, so what each setting does after a positive screen is taken from the information sheet.

sources.cite: The Columbia Lighthouse Project, Columbia Protocol (C-SSRS) triage page: 'the most worrisome answers are a recent (past month) yes to items 4 or 5' (intent, intent with a plan) 'and/or any recent (3 months) behavior'; next steps 'are setting specific', and 'interventions should be changed to reflect your individual resources and policies'
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 (summarizing fetch with quotes; page last modified 2024-03-22). The screener's items, relayed from the NCMHCE session (read 2026-11-11): wish to be dead; suicidal thoughts; thoughts with method; intent without plan; intent with plan; suicidal behavior.

sources.cite: The Joint Commission, R3 Report Issue 18: National Patient Safety Goal for suicide prevention, NPSG.15.01.01 (effective 2019-07-01): EP1 environmental risk assessment; EP2 screen 'using a validated screening tool'; EP3 an assessment that 'directly asks about suicidal ideation, plan, intent, suicidal or self-harm behaviors'; EP4 document the risk level and the mitigation plan; EP5-EP7 policies for monitoring, discharge counseling and follow-up
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 (summarizing fetch with quotes; issue dated 2019-11-20, updated 2025-12-03). The report names one-to-one monitoring as a key protocol on nonpsychiatric units; it does not itself require it, so the observation level in each sim is the facility's policy.

brief.situation: Walter Brandt, 74 (a fictional patient), is at your clinic for a blood pressure check. His wife of 48 years died in June. He drove himself here and lives alone; his son lives across town. His blood pressure is at goal. When you ask how he has been managing, he says, 'Since June, nothing's the same. I've been getting things in order.' The clinic uses the NIMH Ask Suicide-Screening Questions when there is a cue. You are his family nurse practitioner, with 30 minutes for the visit.
handover: Blood pressure at goal; no medication changes needed.

Clinic policy: an acute positive screen is an emergency referral. The patient stays in sight of staff and is taken for an emergency evaluation by ambulance or the mobile crisis team, never driving himself, with a call ahead to the receiving team.
howItWorks: Choose what to ask and how to respond from the action groups. Walter answers at once; then let the conversation continue, which moves the clock by the minutes that exchange took.
His trust, distress and how much he discloses change with what you say.
The visit ends at 30 minutes. Afterward you write a short risk formulation, then document the risk level and disposition.

source.note: A 30-minute primary care visit (author's scenario timing).
How trust and distress move with each response is a teaching simplification for exam practice, not a validated model of a patient.

checkIn.label: Open: 'Tell me about getting things in order.'

effects.log: You put down the chart and ask him what he means by getting things in order.

effects.finding: "The will. The house. Who gets the watch." He looks at his hands.

reflect.label: Reflect what you hear (empathic reflection)
reflect.why: You have reflected a lot already; move on.

effects.log: You reflect the feeling under what was said, without judging it.

effects.finding: He nods. "That's it. Fifty years, and then quiet."

normalize.label: Normalize: 'When someone has lost what you've lost, I ask some direct questions. It's safe to answer.'

effects.log: You say you ask some direct questions of anyone carrying a loss like his, and that it is safe to answer.

screen.label: Screen with the NIMH Ask Suicide-Screening Questions (the four questions)
screen.why: He has answered; go on to the follow-up questions.

effects.log: You ask the four screening questions directly.

then.finding: "Yes. Yes. And yes, I think about killing myself most days." No past attempt.

then.log: Positive screen: a wish to be dead, feeling a burden, suicidal thoughts this week; no past attempt.

then.finding: "I'm fine. Just old." (Not yet enough trust to answer honestly.)

formulation.question: Write your risk formulation for Walter: his risk level and why, and what you put in place.

parts.label: Risk level and reasons
parts.criteria: Names an acute positive screen, imminent risk: thoughts right now, a plan and a time, intent, access at home, preparation ('getting things in order'); risk factors: recent bereavement, older man living alone; protective: his son and grandson.
parts.modelAnswer: Acute positive: thoughts of killing himself right now, a plan for this weekend, stated intent, access at home and putting his affairs in order. An older widower living alone four months after his wife's death. His son and grandson are protective but not enough today.

parts.label: What was put in place
parts.criteria: Names keeping him in sight, an emergency evaluation today by ambulance or crisis team rather than driving, a call ahead with a handoff, and his son told with consent.
parts.modelAnswer: He stayed in sight of staff; an emergency evaluation today by ambulance under the clinic policy, not driving; a call ahead with a handoff to the emergency department; Karl called with his consent and meeting him there.

source.note: Trust at the close of the conversation.
His words are a cue present from the first minute; screening within 15 minutes leaves time to arrange an emergency evaluation inside the visit (author's scenario timing).

expertPath.text: Ask what 'getting things in order' means; reflect; normalize; screen.
The acuity question; plan and intent without details; access; who he is close to.

safe.headline: Good: on his way to an evaluation
safe.body: You heard the cue in 'getting things in order', screened, asked the acuity question and acted on an acute positive the way the policy sets out.

safeGaps.headline: Evaluated, with gaps
safeGaps.body: Walter got to an evaluation, but the criteria below show what was late or missing.

unsafe.headline: Left at foreseeable risk
unsafe.body: An acute positive screen is an emergency: the patient stays in sight and goes for an evaluation safely, today. The most useful kind of run to learn from.

walkout.headline: The conversation broke
walkout.body: Telling a grieving man he would never do it closes the door. Ask what he means, and then ask directly.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: Nothing was documented before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: 'Getting things in order' after a loss is a warning sign and a cue to screen. A yes to the acuity question is an acute positive: imminent risk, and suicidal intent is a red flag for emergency referral. He stays in sight, goes by ambulance or the crisis team rather than driving, the receiving team gets a call ahead and his son is told with his consent; outpatient treatment alone is not enough today.
